laws.title: Distracted Driving — Handheld Phone Ban
laws.subtitle: FL Statute §316.305 — $30–$158 fine + points
laws.fullDescription: Florida's Wireless Communications While Driving Law (2019) bans texting while driving as a primary offense ($30 first offense). Handheld device use in school/work zones is a primary offense ($158 + 3 points). Hands-free is always permitted.
laws.penalty: 1st offense (texting): $30 + court costs. School/work zone violation: $158 + 3 demerit points.
exceptions: Stationary vehicle (not in traffic)
Emergency calls to 911
Law enforcement on duty

quiz.q: Fine for a first-offense handheld device violation in a school zone in Florida?
quiz.explanation: Handheld device use in a Florida school zone carries a $158 fine plus 3 demerit points.

laws.title: Open Container in Vehicles — Zero Tolerance
laws.subtitle: FL Statute §316.1936 — Non-criminal but costly
laws.fullDescription: It is illegal to possess an open container of alcohol in a motor vehicle in Florida. Applies to both driver and passengers. 'Open' means any container with a broken seal. Conviction is a non-criminal traffic infraction but carries fines.
laws.penalty: $90–$113.50 fine for first violation. Charged to the driver if passenger container found.
exceptions: Passengers in for-hire vehicles (taxis, limos, party buses)
Living quarters of a motor home

quiz.q: Who gets charged if an open container is found with a passenger in Florida?
options: Neither if stopped at red light
quiz.explanation: In Florida, the driver is charged for any open container found in the vehicle, even if it belongs to a passenger.

laws.title: Florida Culture — Outdoor Lifestyle & Diversity
laws.subtitle: Relaxed, warm, multicultural — no one is from Florida
laws.fullDescription: Florida is one of the most diverse states in the US, with large Cuban, Haitian, Puerto Rican, and Jamaican communities — especially in Miami. The culture is relaxed and outdoors-oriented year-round. The phrase 'no one is actually from Florida' reflects its transient population. In South Florida, Spanish is widely spoken alongside English. Tipping is expected (20%+), and the heat dominates social schedules.
laws.penalty: No legal penalty — being dismissive of Florida's diversity or the heat will not go over well.
exceptions: North Florida (the Panhandle) has a distinctly Southern culture closer to Georgia/Alabama
Tampa/Orlando are more Midwestern in character

quiz.q: Which language is widely spoken alongside English in South Florida?
quiz.explanation: Spanish is widely spoken alongside English throughout South Florida, particularly in Miami, driven by large Cuban and broader Latin American communities.

laws.title: Wildlife Laws — Alligators and Protected Species
laws.subtitle: FWC — Never feed alligators; $500 fine; felony for killing
laws.fullDescription: Florida has strict wildlife laws, especially around alligators (there are approximately 1.3 million in the state). Feeding alligators is a second-degree misdemeanour — it causes them to lose fear of humans and leads to attacks. Removing or killing an alligator without a permit is a felony. Manatees are federally protected — intentionally touching or harassing a manatee carries federal charges. Sea turtle nesting beaches have lighting ordinances (no bright lights visible from beach during nesting season). Florida panthers, gopher tortoises, and scrub jays are protected species.
laws.penalty: Feeding alligators: $500 fine. Killing gopher tortoise: up to $5,000 fine + 5 years imprisonment. Harassing manatee: federal misdemeanour + $50,000 fine.
exceptions: FWC-licensed nuisance alligator trappers
Permitted wildlife researchers
laws.sourceLabel: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission

quiz.q: What is the penalty for feeding an alligator in Florida?
options: No penalty — alligators are not protected
quiz.explanation: Feeding alligators in Florida is a second-degree misdemeanour carrying a $500 fine — fed alligators lose fear of humans and become dangerous.

laws.title: Beach Access Rights — Florida's Public Beach Access Law
laws.subtitle: Florida Doctrine of Custom — Most beaches publicly accessible
laws.fullDescription: Florida recognises the 'Doctrine of Custom' for beach access — historically, Florida's beaches above the mean high-tide line have been publicly accessible even if the adjacent land is private. In 2018, the Florida Supreme Court upheld in Alford v. Finch that customary use of beaches is constitutionally permitted. However, access to the beach (the route through private property) is not guaranteed — you cannot trespass on private dunes or property to get there. Beaches cannot be blocked by private owners from customary public use.
laws.penalty: Blocking customary public beach access: civil injunction + legal challenge. Trespassing through private property to reach beach: trespass charge.
exceptions: Some private resort beaches restrict access at high-tide line
Beach access points (public boardwalks) are designated by county
laws.sourceLabel: Florida Statute §163.035 — Beach and Dune Customary Use

quiz.q: Can private Florida beach property owners fully close off a beach to the public?
options: Yes — private property rights are absolute
No — Florida's Doctrine of Custom means beaches with historical public use remain publicly accessible
Yes — if they post proper signage
quiz.explanation: Florida's Doctrine of Custom means that beaches with a history of public use remain accessible even adjacent to private property — though you still cannot trespass through private land to reach them.

laws.title: Alligator and Wildlife Interaction Laws
laws.subtitle: Florida Fish and Wildlife Code — Feeding alligators is illegal
laws.fullDescription: Florida has the largest alligator population in the USA — about 1.3 million. Feeding wild alligators is illegal under Florida law: fed alligators associate humans with food and become dangerous, requiring removal and euthanasia. Harassing, capturing, or killing wild alligators without a permit is also illegal. Florida has a licensed Statewide Nuisance Alligator Program (SNAP) that handles nuisance gators. Pythons (Burmese pythons, an invasive species in the Everglades) may actually be legally killed by anyone with a hunting licence — part of Florida's python elimination programme.
laws.penalty: Feeding a wild alligator: $500 fine + possible imprisonment. Harassing or killing an alligator without permit: up to $500 fine + 60 days imprisonment.
exceptions: Licensed alligator trappers under SNAP programme
FWC officers and licensed researchers
Python elimination — Burmese pythons may be killed humanely by anyone with a licence
laws.sourceLabel: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission — Alligator Rules

quiz.q: Why is feeding wild alligators illegal in Florida?
options: Fed alligators associate humans with food, become dangerous, and must be euthanised
quiz.explanation: Feeding wild alligators in Florida is illegal because it causes them to lose their natural fear of humans — they become dangerous nuisances that must then be removed and euthanised. The law protects both people and the alligators.

laws.title: Alligator Feeding Ban — Feeding Gators Creates Dangerous Habituated Animals
laws.subtitle: Florida Statute §379.2426 — Criminal offence to feed wild alligators
laws.fullDescription: Florida is home to over 1.3 million wild American alligators. It is a second-degree misdemeanor under Florida Statute §379.2426 to feed or entice wild alligators. The reason: a fed gator loses its fear of humans and quickly becomes a public safety hazard — the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission (FWC) then has no choice but to euthanise it. 'A fed gator is a dead gator' is FWC's slogan. Florida also prohibits harassing, capturing, or killing alligators without a permit. Despite their fearsome reputation, alligators rarely attack humans — habituated animals account for nearly all serious incidents.
laws.penalty: Feeding a wild alligator: class 2 misdemeanor — up to 60 days jail + $500 fine. Nuisance alligator trapping without licence: up to $500 fine.
exceptions: Licensed alligator trappers hired by FWC for nuisance removal
Alligator farms and licensed wildlife educators
laws.sourceLabel: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission — Alligator Facts

quiz.q: Approximately how many wild American alligators live in Florida?
quiz.explanation: Florida is home to approximately 1.3 million wild American alligators — they live in all 67 counties and can appear in swimming pools, golf courses, and residential ponds.

laws.title: Stand Your Ground Law — Florida's Controversial Self-Defence Statute
laws.subtitle: Florida Statute §776.013 — No duty to retreat; deadly force justified in many contexts
laws.fullDescription: Florida's 'Stand Your Ground' law (Florida Statute §776.013, enacted 2005) allows a person who believes they are in imminent danger to use force — including deadly force — without first retreating. Unlike most states' self-defence laws, there is no duty to retreat if you are in a place you have a legal right to be. This law gained national attention during the 2012 Trayvon Martin case. 'Stand Your Ground' hearings (immunity hearings) can result in criminal charges being dismissed. Florida also has a 'Warning Shot' law (2014) that protects people who fire warning shots in self-defence. Visitors should be aware that Florida residents may be armed (concealed carry is common).
laws.penalty: Using force beyond what is legally justified: criminal prosecution for assault, battery, or murder. Firearms in Florida without proper licence (for non-residents): criminal charge.
exceptions: Law enforcement officers acting in official capacity
Licensed concealed carry permit holders following all applicable rules

quiz.q: In what year did Florida enact its 'Stand Your Ground' self-defence law?
quiz.explanation: Florida enacted its 'Stand Your Ground' law in 2005, allowing people to use force without retreating if they believe they face imminent danger — it became nationally controversial after the 2012 Trayvon Martin shooting.

laws.title: Florida Manatee Protection Zones — Speed Restrictions; No-Entry Areas
laws.subtitle: Federal and Florida law protect endangered West Indian manatees in waterways
laws.fullDescription: The West Indian manatee is protected under both the U.S. Endangered Species Act and Florida's Manatee Sanctuary Act (Chapter 379 F.S.). Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission designates slow-speed, minimum-wake, and no-entry zones in waterways where manatees aggregate, particularly in winter near warm water springs. Boat operators must reduce to idle/no-wake speed in posted manatee zones. Feeding or giving water to manatees (even fresh water) is illegal, as it alters their natural behavior. Swimming with manatees is permitted only in Crystal River area under strict 'passive observation' rules — no chasing, encircling, or riding. Violations are reported via a hotline (1-888-404-FWCC).
laws.penalty: Harassing manatees: fines up to $50,000 + 1 year imprisonment (federal). Boating violations in manatee zones: $250–$500 per offense. Commercial captains: license revocation.
exceptions: Authorized manatee rescue operations
Scientific research under federal and state permits
Law enforcement vessels in emergencies

quiz.q: Why is it illegal to give manatees fresh water in Florida?
options: Fresh water is harmful to their kidneys
It alters their natural behavior and makes them dependent on humans
It attracts too many manatees to boat areas
quiz.explanation: Feeding or providing fresh water to manatees is illegal in Florida because it conditions them to seek out humans and boats for food/water, altering their natural foraging behavior and increasing boat strike risk.

laws.title: Florida's 'Don't Say Gay' Law — Parental Rights in Education Act
laws.subtitle: Florida's 2022 law restricts LGBTQ+ classroom discussion; expanded in 2023 to all grade levels
laws.fullDescription: Florida's Parental Rights in Education Act (HB 1557, 2022) — nicknamed 'Don't Say Gay' by critics — prohibits classroom instruction on sexual orientation or gender identity in kindergarten through grade 3, and requires that any instruction in higher grades be 'age appropriate.' The 2023 expansion extended these restrictions to all grade levels (K–12). Teachers and schools face lawsuits from parents for violations. The law led to removals of classroom library books, self-censorship by teachers, and resignation of LGBTQ+ educators. Disney publicly opposed the law, triggering a protracted legal dispute with Governor DeSantis over Disney's special district status. Civil rights groups filed lawsuits arguing First Amendment and equal protection violations. Multiple other states passed similar laws following Florida's lead.
laws.penalty: School districts violating the law: loss of state funding. Individual teacher violations: license discipline proceedings. Schools: subject to parental lawsuits with legal fees.
exceptions: General anti-bullying education may still mention LGBTQ+ students
Health education covering biological reproduction (limited)
Student-led discussions or student-created content (contested)
laws.sourceLabel: Florida Senate — HB 1557 Parental Rights in Education Act 2022

quiz.q: What company publicly opposed Florida's 'Don't Say Gay' law and subsequently had a major legal dispute with Governor DeSantis?
quiz.explanation: Disney publicly opposed Florida's Parental Rights in Education Act, leading Governor DeSantis to dissolve Disney's special tax district (Reedy Creek Improvement District) in retaliation — triggering a prolonged legal and political battle between Florida's government and one of its largest employers and tax contributors.

laws.title: Florida Man Laws — Unusual Florida Statutes and the 'Florida Man' Phenomenon
laws.subtitle: Florida's unusual laws and lack of a state income tax combine to create unique legal landscape
laws.fullDescription: Florida's legal system has several genuinely unusual features that contribute to the 'Florida Man' internet meme. Florida's Government in the Sunshine Law (Chapter 286) and Public Records Law (Chapter 119) are among America's most expansive open government laws — virtually all government records and meetings are public, including arrest records, creating a firehose of unusual crime stories accessible to journalists. Florida has no state income tax (enshrined in the Florida Constitution since 1924) — a major draw for wealthy retirees and businesses, but creating pressure on property taxes and fees. Florida's Stand Your Ground Law (2005) allows using deadly force wherever a person has a legal right to be, without duty to retreat. Florida's homestead exemption protects primary homes from most debt collection — making Florida attractive to those seeking asset protection.
laws.penalty: Violating Government in the Sunshine: voiding of actions taken in illegal meetings + personal fines up to $500. Stand Your Ground misuse: criminal prosecution for unjustified force.
exceptions: National security and active law enforcement investigations have public records exemptions
Personal information in arrest records can be requested for redaction in limited circumstances
Homestead exemption does not protect against mortgage debt or property tax liens
laws.sourceLabel: Florida Division of Elections — Government in the Sunshine Law

quiz.q: Why does Florida produce so many bizarre crime news stories compared to other US states?
options: Florida has the highest crime rate per capita of any US state
Florida's extensive public records law makes virtually all arrest records accessible to journalists
Florida lacks a public defender system so all cases go to trial
Florida's warm climate attracts more criminal activity
quiz.explanation: Florida's Government in the Sunshine Law (Public Records Law) makes virtually all government records — including arrest records — immediately publicly accessible. This creates a uniquely searchable database of Florida crimes that journalists and internet users can access, generating the 'Florida Man' meme. Other states have similar crimes but not the same public accessibility of records.

laws.title: Parental Rights in Education ('Don't Say Gay') Law
laws.subtitle: Florida banned LGBTQ+ instruction in K-3 classrooms, later extended to all grades
laws.fullDescription: Florida's Parental Rights in Education Act (HB 1557, 2022) — dubbed 'Don't Say Gay' by critics — prohibited classroom instruction on sexual orientation and gender identity for students in grades K–3. A 2023 expansion extended the restriction through grade 12 unless 'age-appropriate.' Teachers and school staff faced potential dismissal for violation. The law prompted Disney to publicly oppose it, triggering Governor DeSantis's retaliatory takeover of Disney's self-governing Reedy Creek Improvement District (later reversed after legal battle). The law became a national symbol of education culture wars and inspired similar legislation in dozens of other states.
laws.penalty: Teachers violating the law face dismissal proceedings. Schools can be sued by parents. Districts face loss of state funding for non-compliance.
exceptions: Health education required by law is exempt
Incidental, non-instructional references are not prohibited
High school instruction allowed if deemed developmentally appropriate under 2023 expansion
laws.sourceLabel: Florida Senate — HB 1557 Parental Rights in Education

quiz.q: What corporate backlash against Florida's 'Don't Say Gay' law did Governor DeSantis retaliate against?
options: Disney publicly opposed the law, leading DeSantis to target its self-governing district
Netflix moved headquarters out of Florida
quiz.explanation: Disney's public opposition to Florida's 'Don't Say Gay' law prompted Governor DeSantis to retaliate by taking over Disney's self-governing Reedy Creek Improvement District — a corporate governance battle that ended in a legal settlement reversing the takeover.

laws.title: Red Tide Crisis & Lake Okeechobee Discharges
laws.subtitle: Florida's toxic algae blooms killed fish and harmed tourism — tied to sugar industry pollution
laws.fullDescription: Florida's recurring red tide (Karenia brevis) and blue-green algae crises have caused massive environmental and economic damage. In 2018, a catastrophic algae bloom — fed by Lake Okeechobee discharges carrying nutrient-laden water from sugar farmlands — spread throughout the Caloosahatchee and St. Lucie rivers, killing fish, dolphins, and manatees, closing beaches, and costing Southwest Florida hundreds of millions in tourism losses. The Army Corps of Engineers' management of Lake Okeechobee discharges is central to the crisis. The Comprehensive Everglades Restoration Plan (authorized 2000) aims to store and clean water before discharge but remains decades behind schedule.
laws.penalty: Illegal discharge of pollutants: EPA civil penalties up to $70,117/day per violation. Violations of National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System permits: criminal fines and imprisonment. Agricultural runoff regulations under Florida's Clean Water Act are enforced by FDEP.
exceptions: The 'Farming right to farm' law limits nuisance claims against existing agricultural operations
Agricultural stormwater management has reduced (not eliminated) discharge requirements
Emergency discharges from Lake Okeechobee to prevent levee failure override pollution rules
laws.sourceLabel: Florida Department of Environmental Protection — HABs

quiz.q: What is the primary nutrient source blamed for feeding Florida's toxic algae blooms?
options: Phosphorus and nitrogen from agricultural land draining into Lake Okeechobee
Industrial chemicals from Tampa Bay refineries
quiz.explanation: Phosphorus and nitrogen from agricultural lands (primarily sugar farms) draining into Lake Okeechobee are the primary nutrient sources feeding Florida's toxic algae blooms — with Army Corps of Engineers discharges carrying this nutrient-laden water to coastal waterways.

laws.title: Parental Rights in Education Act ('Don't Say Gay' Law)
laws.subtitle: Florida's 2022 law restricts LGBTQ+ classroom discussion and sparked a national culture war
laws.fullDescription: Florida's Parental Rights in Education Act (HB 1557), signed by Governor DeSantis in March 2022 and nicknamed 'Don't Say Gay' by critics, prohibits classroom instruction on sexual orientation or gender identity in kindergarten through grade 3 and requires 'age-appropriate' content in higher grades. The law allows parents to sue school districts for violations. It was expanded in 2023 to cover all grades K–12, effectively prohibiting classroom discussion of LGBTQ+ topics in all public schools. Dozens of other states subsequently passed similar laws. Disney, which initially stayed silent before criticizing the law, had its special self-governing district revoked by the state in a highly publicized dispute with DeSantis.
laws.penalty: School districts face lawsuits from parents. Teachers can be reported and face discipline for violations. Districts risk loss of state funding
exceptions: Incidental discussion triggered by student questions may be handled differently
Books with LGBTQ+ content are subject to review and removal from school libraries
laws.sourceLabel: Florida Senate – HB 1557 Parental Rights in Education

quiz.q: What company became publicly embroiled in a dispute with Florida Governor DeSantis over the 'Don't Say Gay' law?
quiz.explanation: Disney initially stayed silent on HB 1557 before criticizing it after employee pressure. Governor DeSantis retaliated by dissolving Disney's special self-governing Reedy Creek Improvement District — sparking a prolonged legal and political battle.

laws.title: Florida's Property Rights Amendment & Stand Your Ground Expansion
laws.subtitle: Florida expanded 'Stand Your Ground' to presume shooters acted lawfully — shifting the burden of proof from defense to prosecution
laws.fullDescription: Florida's Stand Your Ground law (2005) originally removed the duty to retreat before using force in self-defense, if a person is in a place they have a lawful right to be. In 2017, Florida amended the law to shift the burden of proof: instead of the defendant proving self-defense at a pretrial hearing, prosecutors must now prove the claim of self-defense is not valid — a fundamental reversal of normal legal procedure. Florida's law gained national attention after the 2012 Trayvon Martin shooting, in which George Zimmerman was acquitted citing Stand Your Ground. Critics argue the law has enabled racially disparate outcomes: studies found white defendants who kill Black victims are significantly more likely to have Stand Your Ground claims succeed.
laws.penalty: If Stand Your Ground applies: immunity from prosecution and civil suit. If it doesn't apply: standard homicide/assault charges. Wrongful use of force: standard criminal penalties
exceptions: Stand Your Ground does not apply if the person was engaged in criminal activity at the time
Mutual combat situations limit Stand Your Ground claims

quiz.q: What significant change did Florida make to its Stand Your Ground law in 2017?
options: It expanded the law to cover threats, not just physical attacks
It shifted the burden of proof to prosecutors to disprove self-defense claims, rather than defendants proving them
It added a 48-hour cooling-off period before charges could be filed
It required mandatory mediation before prosecution
quiz.explanation: Florida's 2017 amendment shifted the burden of proof at pretrial immunity hearings: instead of defendants proving self-defense, prosecutors must now prove the self-defense claim is invalid — a fundamental reversal that makes Stand Your Ground protections significantly harder to overcome.

laws.title: Gator Feeding Ban
laws.subtitle: Feeding wild alligators in Florida is illegal — and dangerous
laws.fullDescription: Florida Statute 372.667 prohibits feeding wild alligators or crocodiles. The law exists because alligators that are fed by humans lose their natural fear of people and begin associating humans with food, greatly increasing the risk of attack. These 'nuisance' alligators must then be trapped and destroyed by Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission (FWC) contractors. With over 1.3 million alligators in Florida, the state has the world's largest alligator population. FWC receives approximately 17,000 nuisance alligator complaints per year.
laws.penalty: Up to $500 fine and/or 60 days in jail; repeat offenders face higher penalties
exceptions: Licensed alligator farmers and research facilities are exempt
FWC officers may feed alligators for research or relocation purposes
laws.sourceLabel: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission

quiz.q: Why does feeding wild alligators make them MORE dangerous?
options: They lose their natural fear of humans and associate people with food
It causes them to migrate toward populated areas
quiz.explanation: Fed alligators lose their instinctive fear of humans and begin associating people with food. This 'habituation' dramatically increases attack risk, which is why feeding is illegal in Florida.

laws.title: Homestead Exemption Law
laws.subtitle: Florida's constitution protects primary residences from unlimited property tax increases
laws.fullDescription: Florida's 'Save Our Homes' Amendment (1992) caps annual increases in assessed value of homestead (primary residence) properties at 3% or the Consumer Price Index, whichever is lower. This means long-term homeowners pay far less property tax than new buyers of comparable homes — a phenomenon called 'lock-in effect.' Florida also has an unlimited homestead exemption from creditor claims (Article X, Section 4 of Florida Constitution) — meaning a primary residence cannot be seized to satisfy most debts, regardless of its value. This has historically attracted wealthy debtors to Florida; OJ Simpson moved to Florida after his civil trial judgment specifically to protect his home.
laws.penalty: Fraudulent homestead claims: back taxes plus 50% penalty plus interest; property tax fraud: criminal charges
exceptions: Investment properties and vacation homes are not protected
Federal tax liens can attach to homesteaded property

quiz.q: What does Florida's unlimited homestead exemption protect against?
options: Seizure of your primary home by most creditors
quiz.explanation: Florida's constitutional homestead exemption protects a primary residence from seizure by most creditors regardless of value — making Florida a popular destination for people facing large civil judgments, as their home cannot be taken.

laws.title: Manatee Protection Law
laws.subtitle: Florida law protects manatees with strict boating speed zones
laws.fullDescription: Florida's Manatee Sanctuary Act (1978, updated) designates Florida's coastal and freshwater areas as a state manatee sanctuary. Boat speed zones — Idle Speed/No Wake, Slow Speed, and Minimum Wake — are legally mandated around areas where manatees congregate (warm water springs, power plant outflow canals). Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission (FWC) enforces these zones with zero tolerance. Manatees are protected under federal Endangered Species Act and Marine Mammal Protection Act. As of 2023, Florida's manatee population has recovered to approximately 8,000 — from a low of 1,267 in 1991. Boat strikes remain the leading cause of death.
laws.penalty: Speeding in manatee zones: federal and state fines up to $50,000; injuring a manatee: federal charges — up to $100,000 fine and 1 year imprisonment
exceptions: Emergency vessels responding to incidents may exceed speed limits
Research vessels with permits can work in no-entry zones

quiz.q: Approximately how many manatees live in Florida's waters today?
quiz.explanation: Florida's manatee population has recovered to approximately 8,000 individuals as of 2023 — up from a low of 1,267 in 1991 — due largely to boating speed zone enforcement, warm-water refuge protection, and reduced hunting.

laws.title: Stop WOKE Act and Education Content Laws
laws.subtitle: Florida's laws restricting diversity training and classroom content sparked national controversy
laws.fullDescription: Florida's Individual Freedom Act (commonly called the 'Stop WOKE Act,' enacted 2022) and related legislation under Governor Ron DeSantis represent a major effort to restrict diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) content in workplaces, schools, and universities. Key provisions: employers cannot require employees to attend training that makes them feel guilty for actions of their race/sex; K-12 schools cannot teach 'critical race theory' or instruction that makes students feel guilty for historical events; the Stop WOKE Act restricted how Florida public universities could address race and gender. Federal courts struck down the workplace and university provisions as unconstitutional free speech violations (11th Circuit, 2022–2023), while some K-12 provisions survived. SB 266 (2023) banned DEI programs at public universities and restricted gender studies courses. Florida also enacted the 'Don't Say Gay' law (Parental Rights in Education Act, 2022) limiting instruction on sexual orientation and gender identity.
laws.penalty: Employers violating Stop WOKE Act: civil suits by employees; schools violating classroom instruction laws: loss of state funding; universities maintaining banned DEI programs: funding penalties
exceptions: Private schools are exempt from public school curriculum restrictions
Federal courts have blocked enforcement of some provisions
Historical instruction that presents facts without promoting racial guilt is permitted

laws.title: Live Local Act and Affordable Housing Preemption
laws.subtitle: Florida's 2023 Live Local Act overrides local zoning to allow affordable housing in commercial areas
laws.fullDescription: Florida's Live Local Act (SB 102, signed March 2023) represents a significant state preemption of local zoning authority to address the state's severe housing affordability crisis (Florida had among the fastest-rising rents in the US from 2020–2022, with Miami rents rising 50%+). Key provisions: developers can build residential projects of 40 or more affordable units on any commercial, industrial, or mixed-use property as of right, even if local zoning prohibits it; the state preempts local limits on density and height for such projects; local governments must approve these projects within 30 days; the law allocates $711 million for affordable housing programs; and rent control is specifically preempted (overriding Miami-Dade County's 2022 voter-approved rent control measure). The preemption of Miami-Dade's rent control referendum — passed by 65% of voters — raised constitutional questions about home rule and voter rights. Live Local was expanded in 2024 (SB 328).
laws.penalty: Local governments that refuse to approve qualifying Live Local projects: developer can bring action for damages and attorney fees; municipalities that enact rent control: state preemption action
exceptions: Projects in historic districts may face additional review
Properties within 1 mile of military installations have special review requirements
Live Local does not apply to single-family residential zones

laws.title: Stop WOKE Act and Classroom Content Restrictions
laws.subtitle: Florida restricted how race, gender, and diversity topics are taught
laws.fullDescription: Florida's Individual Freedom Act, nicknamed the 'Stop WOKE Act,' was signed by Governor Ron DeSantis in 2022. It prohibited schools and employers from teaching or training content that makes individuals feel guilt or discomfort based on race, sex, or national origin. Simultaneously, HB 1467 required school libraries to vet and remove books until reviewed by certified media specialists, leading to widespread removals including classics like 'And Tango Makes Three' and works by Toni Morrison. The Parental Rights in Education Act ('Don't Say Gay') restricted classroom instruction on sexual orientation and gender identity in K-3 and limited it beyond that. Federal courts blocked parts of the Stop WOKE Act as unconstitutional under the First Amendment.
laws.penalty: School violations of book or curriculum rules: loss of state funding. Classroom discussion violations: disciplinary action for teachers, potential decertification.
exceptions: Historical instruction on slavery, civil rights, and Holocaust not prohibited
Discussion of biological differences between males and females permitted
Age-appropriate health education allowed in secondary schools

quiz.q: What was Florida's Stop WOKE Act designed to prevent?
options: Teaching content that causes racial or gender-based guilt or discomfort in schools and workplaces
Transgender athletes competing in public school sports
Critical race theory being used in legal proceedings
quiz.explanation: The Stop WOKE Act prohibited instruction or training that causes individuals to feel guilt, anguish, or discomfort based on their race, sex, or national origin.

laws.title: Florida Book Removals and HB 1467 Library Challenges
laws.subtitle: Florida's new vetting law led to thousands of books being pulled from school shelves
laws.fullDescription: Florida's HB 1467 (2022) required that all books in school libraries be vetted and approved by a certified district media specialist before being available to students. During the vetting process, books had to be removed. The result was that thousands of books — including classical literature, award-winning children's books, and works addressing LGBTQ+ themes, race, or history — were pulled from shelves pending review. In some districts, empty shelves were photographed and went viral. Federal courts issued mixed rulings; the 11th Circuit partially upheld Florida's authority to curate school libraries while finding certain removals motivated by viewpoint violated the First Amendment. National PEN America documented over 3,000 book bans in Florida in 2022-2023.
laws.penalty: School administrator allowing non-vetted books: loss of state funding and potential professional discipline. First Amendment violations in book removal: civil damages in federal suits.
exceptions: Classroom instructional materials subject to separate adoption process
Books available in public libraries (non-school) not affected by HB 1467

quiz.q: What did Florida's HB 1467 require that led to mass book removals from school libraries?
options: School boards to vote on each book individually in public session
All library books to be vetted by a certified media specialist — removed pending review
Parents to sign consent forms before students could access any library book
Libraries to replace all books published before 2010
quiz.explanation: HB 1467 required all books in school libraries to be vetted by a certified district media specialist before being available — meaning thousands were removed pending review, leading to empty shelves in many Florida schools.

laws.title: Florida's Property Insurance Crisis and Legislative Reform
laws.subtitle: Florida's homeowners insurance market collapsed, with insurers fleeing the state
laws.fullDescription: Florida experienced a catastrophic property insurance market failure in 2022-2024. Multiple private insurers became insolvent or left Florida, leaving Citizens Property Insurance (the state's insurer of last resort) as the largest insurer — growing to 1.4 million policies at its peak. Insurance premiums tripled and quadrupled for many homeowners. The crisis stemmed from: high hurricane risk, assignment of benefits (AOB) abuse by contractors, excessive litigation, and reinsurance costs. Florida's legislature passed major reforms (SB 2A 2022, SB 2B, and subsequent bills) eliminating one-way attorney fees in insurance suits, reforming AOB, and tightening claims deadlines. The insurance market began stabilizing but premiums remained extremely high.
laws.penalty: Insurance fraud (inflated claims, contractor fraud): up to 30 years depending on amount. AOB violations after reform: unfair trade practice sanctions.
exceptions: Citizens Insurance has a 'depopulation' mandate to remove policies as private market stabilizes
Flood insurance remains through separate federal NFIP program — not affected by state reforms

quiz.q: What is 'Citizens Property Insurance' in Florida and why did it grow dramatically?
options: Florida's largest private insurer that expanded aggressively
The state's insurer of last resort that grew to 1.4 million policies as private insurers fled
A federal program providing subsidized flood insurance
A Citizens' advocacy group fighting insurance rate increases
quiz.explanation: Citizens Property Insurance is Florida's state-run insurer of last resort — intended only as a backstop. As private insurers became insolvent or left Florida due to losses and litigation costs, Citizens grew to 1.4 million policies, becoming the state's largest insurer and exposing taxpayers to massive hurricane liability.

laws.title: Florida's Social Media Age Restrictions
laws.subtitle: Florida banned minors under 14 from social media platforms
laws.fullDescription: Florida's Social Media Use by Minors (HB 3, signed 2024) prohibits children under 14 from creating social media accounts and requires parental consent for 14-15 year olds. Social media platforms must verify the age of Florida users and delete accounts of minors who violate the law. The law was signed by Governor DeSantis. Florida's Digital Bill of Rights (SB 262, 2023) also requires large platforms to give users data deletion rights and prohibits targeted advertising to children. Florida has been aggressive in digital regulation despite being a free-market conservative state.
laws.penalty: Social media platforms violating child age restrictions: fines up to $50,000 per day per violation. Platforms that fail to delete minor accounts upon discovery: fines escalating to $500,000. Willful violations: up to $10,000 per affected minor
exceptions: Messaging apps allowing only direct communications between known users exempt
Online education platforms exempt
Gaming platforms are partially exempt if social features are incidental

quiz.q: What age restriction did Florida's 2024 social media law impose?
options: No one under 16 can have social media accounts
No one under 18 can have social media without parental consent
Children under 14 banned entirely; 14-15 year olds need parental consent
Social media banned for all minors in schools only
quiz.explanation: Florida's 2024 HB 3 banned children under 14 from creating social media accounts entirely, while requiring parental consent for 14-15 year olds — one of the strictest state-level social media age laws in the US.

laws.title: Florida's Education Culture War Laws
laws.subtitle: Book bans, classroom topic restrictions, and AP course controversies
laws.fullDescription: Florida enacted multiple education laws under Governor DeSantis that became nationally controversial. The Parental Rights in Education Act (dubbed 'Don't Say Gay' by opponents) restricted classroom instruction on sexual orientation and gender identity in grades K-12. The Stop WOKE Act restricted diversity, equity, and inclusion training in workplaces and universities. Florida rejected the College Board's AP African American Studies course, required modifications to AP Psychology, and restricted how teachers can discuss race, slavery, and discrimination. Courts blocked some provisions; others remained in effect. Florida's book challenge process led to thousands of books being removed from school libraries.
laws.penalty: Teacher violation of classroom topic restrictions: potential termination and license revocation. Schools failing to comply with book challenge processes: state oversight and funding consequences. DEI programs at public universities: elimination of funding, positions prohibited
exceptions: Private schools not receiving state funding have more flexibility
College courses (not K-12) have somewhat different standards
Factual historical instruction not framed as 'indoctrination' has more protection

quiz.q: What did Florida's Parental Rights in Education Act restrict that earned it the 'Don't Say Gay' nickname?
options: Classroom instruction on sexual orientation and gender identity in all K-12 grades
quiz.explanation: Florida's Parental Rights in Education Act restricted classroom instruction on sexual orientation and gender identity, leading critics to call it the 'Don't Say Gay' law — it initially applied to K-3 grades but was later extended to all K-12 grades.

laws.title: Anti-SLAPP Laws and Free Speech Protections
laws.subtitle: Florida strengthened anti-SLAPP protections for journalists and citizens in 2023
laws.fullDescription: Florida's 2023 HB 991 amended the state's defamation laws and anti-SLAPP (Strategic Lawsuits Against Public Participation) statute. The law creates a higher burden for public figures to prove defamation, requires early dismissal of meritless suits, and allows defendants to recover attorney's fees in SLAPP cases. Anonymous speakers enjoy stronger protections before being unmasked. However, the law also changed the definition of 'actual malice' in ways that some critics say could make it easier to bring defamation claims. The complex changes affect bloggers, journalists, and anyone posting online opinions.
laws.penalty: Anti-SLAPP: defendants who win can recover all attorney's fees and costs from the plaintiff
exceptions: Commercial speech and advertising are not covered
Employment disputes have separate defamation rules

quiz.q: What does SLAPP stand for in legal context?
quiz.explanation: SLAPP stands for Strategic Lawsuit Against Public Participation — lawsuits filed to silence critics, journalists, or activists through expensive litigation.

laws.title: Condo Inspection and Reserve Fund Requirements
laws.subtitle: Florida enacted mandatory condo inspection laws after 2021 Surfside collapse
laws.fullDescription: After the June 2021 Champlain Towers South collapse in Surfside that killed 98 people, Florida passed major condominium safety reforms. SB 4D (2022) and SB 154 (2023) require structural inspections for condominiums three stories or higher every 10 years (beginning after 30 years from original occupancy for buildings near water, 25 years otherwise). Buildings must maintain adequate reserves for major repairs — no longer allowed to waive reserves through owner vote. Non-compliant buildings face restrictions on occupancy and sale. The reforms imposed significant financial burdens on many Florida condo associations.
laws.penalty: Failure to complete required inspections: cannot be sold or collected dues until compliant; inadequate reserves: restrictions on occupancy
exceptions: Single-family homes and buildings under 3 stories
Condos with recently completed comprehensive repairs demonstrating structural adequacy

quiz.q: What triggered Florida's landmark condo inspection law in 2022-2023?
options: The 2021 Champlain Towers South collapse in Surfside that killed 98 people
quiz.explanation: Florida's major condo safety reforms were directly triggered by the June 2021 collapse of Champlain Towers South in Surfside, Florida, which killed 98 people and revealed systemic failures in condo inspection and reserve requirements.

laws.title: Parental Rights in Education Act and Book Restrictions
laws.subtitle: Florida restricted classroom discussion of sexual orientation and gender identity
laws.fullDescription: Florida's Parental Rights in Education Act (HB 1557, 2022), dubbed 'Don't Say Gay' by critics, prohibited classroom instruction on sexual orientation and gender identity in kindergarten through 3rd grade and required such discussions to be 'age-appropriate' in other grades. A 2023 expansion extended the prohibition through 8th grade. Florida also enacted the Individual Freedom Act restricting workplace diversity training and expanded library book review processes resulting in tens of thousands of books being pulled from school shelves for review. The laws were challenged in federal courts on First Amendment grounds, with mixed results.
laws.penalty: School districts violating the instructional restrictions: loss of state funding; libraries with unreviewed books: administrative sanctions
exceptions: Health education and age-appropriate science instruction retain some flexibility
Private schools and home schools operate under different frameworks

quiz.q: What expansion did Florida make to its Parental Rights in Education Act in 2023?
options: Extended the classroom restriction from K-3 through 8th grade
Required parental sign-off for all books
quiz.explanation: Florida's 2023 expansion extended the Parental Rights in Education Act's prohibition on classroom instruction about sexual orientation and gender identity from K-3rd grade through 8th grade.

laws.title: Florida Social Media Age Verification Law
laws.subtitle: Florida bans children under 14 from social media platforms
laws.fullDescription: Florida's HB 3 (2024) prohibits social media platforms from allowing children under 14 to create accounts and requires parental consent for 14- and 15-year-olds. Platforms must use age verification methods and delete accounts of minors who do not meet age requirements. The law survived initial legal challenges and platforms must implement compliance systems.
laws.penalty: Fines up to $50,000 per violation; platforms may be sued by parents of affected minors
exceptions: Email and direct messaging services
Educational platforms
Platforms with fewer than 25 million monthly users

quiz.q: Under Florida's 2024 social media law, what age is the complete ban threshold for creating accounts?
quiz.explanation: Florida's HB 3 bans children under 14 from creating social media accounts entirely and requires parental consent for 14- and 15-year-olds.

laws.title: Florida Live Local Act — Affordable Housing
laws.subtitle: Florida overrides local zoning to increase affordable housing
laws.fullDescription: Florida's Live Local Act (2023) is one of the most significant housing policy reforms in Florida history. It preempts local zoning ordinances to allow affordable housing developments in any area zoned for commercial, industrial, or mixed use — if at least 40% of units are set aside as affordable for 30 years. Local governments cannot impose density limits or height restrictions below the tallest existing building nearby. The law also provides property tax exemptions for qualifying developments.
laws.penalty: Local governments that attempt to block qualifying developments face legal challenge and possible invalidation of their actions
exceptions: Historic districts with additional protections
Areas with environmental constraints
Single-family-only residential zones are not covered

quiz.q: What percentage of units must be set aside as affordable for a development to qualify under Florida's Live Local Act?
quiz.explanation: Florida's Live Local Act requires at least 40% of units in a qualifying development to be designated as affordable housing for a minimum of 30 years.

laws.title: Florida Stop WOKE Act
laws.subtitle: Florida limits diversity training in workplaces and universities
laws.fullDescription: Florida's Stop WOKE Act (Individual Freedom Act, 2022) prohibits employers from requiring employees to attend trainings that promote certain concepts related to race, sex, or national origin, including teachings that individuals bear responsibility for historical discrimination. The law also applies to public universities. Federal courts blocked the university provisions as a violation of the First Amendment, while the workplace provisions went through extended litigation. The law reflected the broader national debate on diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) programs.
laws.penalty: Employers who violate the Act face complaints to the FCHR; employees can sue for damages; public universities face loss of state funding
exceptions: Private universities are not covered
Voluntary DEI activities not requiring employee participation
Historical education about discrimination provided factually

quiz.q: What did federal courts do to Florida's Stop WOKE Act regarding universities?
options: Struck down the university provisions as a First Amendment violation
quiz.explanation: Federal courts blocked the university provisions of Florida's Stop WOKE Act as a violation of the First Amendment's free speech protections, while the workplace provisions were separately litigated.

laws.title: Florida Anti-Squatting Law
laws.subtitle: Florida fast-tracks removal of squatters from private property
laws.fullDescription: Florida enacted a law in 2024 allowing property owners to contact law enforcement to quickly remove squatters from their property without going through a lengthy civil eviction process. The law was in response to cases where organized squatting rings had exploited procedural delays in the eviction process. Property owners provide a sworn statement that the person is squatting, law enforcement can remove them within 24 hours if the squatter cannot produce a lease, rental receipt, or utility bill.
laws.penalty: Squatters who provide false documentation to avoid removal: criminal charges; law enforcement must verify owner's claim before removal
exceptions: Tenants with any form of rental agreement
Holdover tenants must be handled through civil eviction
Disputes about ownership cannot be resolved through the squatter removal process

quiz.q: How quickly can Florida law enforcement remove squatters under the 2024 anti-squatting law?
options: Within 24 hours if the person cannot produce evidence of a rental agreement
quiz.explanation: Florida's 2024 anti-squatting law allows law enforcement to remove people from private property within 24 hours if they cannot produce a lease, rental receipt, or utility bill — bypassing the normal civil eviction process.

laws.title: Stop WOKE Act and Education Restrictions
laws.subtitle: Florida's laws limiting DEI training and classroom topics
laws.fullDescription: Florida's Stop WOKE Act (Individual Freedom Act) prohibits workplace diversity training and school instruction that could make individuals feel guilty based on race, sex, or national origin. Related laws restrict discussion of sexual orientation and gender identity in K-12 classrooms (originally K-3, later challenged and revised), limit AP courses deemed to include prohibited content, give parents rights to review and challenge curriculum materials, and restrict state universities from using funds for DEI programs. The laws have been subject to significant First Amendment litigation.
laws.penalty: Schools and employers violating the Stop WOKE Act face civil lawsuits; state university employees who violate DEI restrictions face employment actions; violations of parental rights law can trigger loss of state funding
exceptions: Age-appropriate factual instruction about historical events including slavery is permitted
Discussion of current events in developmentally appropriate ways is allowed
Scientific teaching about human biology does not implicate the restrictions

quiz.q: What did Florida's Stop WOKE Act primarily target in workplaces and educational settings?
options: Diversity and inclusion training that could make individuals feel guilty based on identity
quiz.explanation: Florida's Stop WOKE Act targeted diversity, equity, and inclusion training and instruction that could cause individuals to feel guilty, distress, or responsibility based on their race, sex, or national origin.

laws.title: Florida Live Local Act
laws.subtitle: Florida's law incentivizing affordable housing near commercial areas
laws.fullDescription: Florida's Live Local Act (HB 543) created significant incentives for affordable housing development. The law prohibits local governments from blocking affordable housing developments in commercial and mixed-use zones if a developer commits to affordable units, preempts local zoning that would prevent density if affordable housing is included, extends property tax exemptions to affordable units in market-rate buildings, and allows local governments to use land for affordable housing. Developers committing a certain percentage of units at affordable rents can build at higher densities than zoning would otherwise allow.
laws.penalty: Local governments that violate Live Local Act preemptions face lawsuits and are liable for developer's attorneys fees; false representations in affordable housing certifications carry civil and criminal penalties
exceptions: Historic districts have modified Live Local Act application
Single-family residential zones have different thresholds
Military installation flight paths may restrict application in certain areas

quiz.q: What zoning authority does Florida's Live Local Act override for affordable housing developers?
options: Local government zoning restrictions in commercial and mixed-use areas
quiz.explanation: Florida's Live Local Act preempts local government zoning restrictions in commercial and mixed-use areas, allowing higher density affordable housing development that would otherwise be blocked by local zoning ordinances — taking the decision away from municipalities.

laws.title: Sea Level Rise Adaptation Plans
laws.subtitle: Florida's coastal construction and climate adaptation regulations
laws.fullDescription: Florida faces severe sea level rise risks, particularly for Miami-Dade, Broward, and Monroe counties. State regulations require coastal construction setback lines, elevation requirements for new construction, special flood hazard area regulations under FEMA's National Flood Insurance Program, and Miami's Building Better Together resilience initiative. Local governments along the coast have enacted stronger elevation requirements. Florida's unique challenge is coastal real estate valued at trillions of dollars in high-risk areas. Governor DeSantis has avoided the term climate change while pursuing adaptation funding.
laws.penalty: Building below required elevation in flood hazard areas makes properties ineligible for flood insurance; coastal construction without permits carries fines and demolition orders; obstructing natural coastal dunes triggers environmental penalties
exceptions: Existing structures built before current code requirements have modified upgrade timelines
Emergency repairs after storm damage have expedited permitting
Agricultural coastal land has different development restrictions from residential

quiz.q: Which Florida counties face the most severe sea level rise risks?
options: Escambia, Santa Rosa, and Okaloosa in the Panhandle
Miami-Dade, Broward, and Monroe in South Florida
Duval, Nassau, and St. Johns in Northeast Florida
Hillsborough, Pinellas, and Pasco in Tampa Bay
quiz.explanation: Miami-Dade, Broward, and Monroe counties in South Florida face the most severe sea level rise risks due to their low elevation, porous limestone geology (which cannot be protected with seawalls like other coastlines), and the enormous value of existing development.

laws.title: Florida Individual Freedom Act ('Stop WOKE Act')
laws.subtitle: Restricting workplace and school critical race theory instruction
laws.fullDescription: Florida's Individual Freedom Act (HB 7, 2022), nicknamed the 'Stop WOKE Act,' prohibits Florida employers, schools, and universities from requiring diversity training that includes certain concepts: that individuals bear collective guilt for historical actions of their race, that individuals are inherently racist, or that meritocracy is racist. Courts have partially struck down the business and higher education provisions as First Amendment violations, while K-12 provisions have received different treatment in federal courts.
laws.penalty: Employers who conduct prohibited training: private civil liability lawsuits with compensatory damages up to $100,000 per incident. Schools that violate the law: loss of state funding and subject to parental lawsuits.
exceptions: Factual instruction about historical discrimination (slavery, civil rights history) permitted as long as it does not attribute present guilt
Voluntary diversity training where employees can opt out without penalty falls outside the prohibition
Training required by federal law (e.g., Title VII harassment training) not subject to the state prohibition

quiz.q: What type of diversity training concept does Florida's Stop WOKE Act specifically prohibit?
options: Training that states individuals bear collective guilt for historical racial actions
Training that acknowledges pay disparities by race
Discussing racial demographics in the workplace
quiz.explanation: Florida's Stop WOKE Act specifically prohibits mandatory training that teaches individuals bear collective racial guilt for historical actions, that meritocracy is racist, or that individuals are inherently racist by virtue of their race — while permitting factual historical instruction.

laws.title: Florida New College Takeover and Higher Education Reform
laws.subtitle: State-appointed trustees transform progressive liberal arts college
laws.fullDescription: Florida Governor DeSantis installed new trustees at New College of Florida in January 2023, who fired the president and hired former Manhattan Institute scholar Christopher Rufo (an architect of the 'anti-woke' movement) and military veterans as administrators, eliminated the gender studies department, ended diversity, equity, and inclusion programs, and radically changed the curriculum. The takeover was part of Florida's broader effort to reshape higher education away from 'leftist indoctrination.' Similar (less dramatic) changes were pursued at other state universities.
laws.penalty: University employees who continue DEI programs after state prohibition: disciplinary action and potential termination under Florida's Individual Freedom Act and Board of Governors regulations. State funding withheld from non-compliant institutions.
exceptions: Private universities in Florida not subject to state DEI prohibitions
Federal Pell Grant recipients retain their aid regardless of state changes to programs
Academic freedom protections for tenured faculty provide some protection against content-based dismissals under Board of Governors rules

quiz.q: Who was hired as a key administrator at New College of Florida after the DeSantis-appointed trustees took over?
quiz.explanation: Christopher Rufo, a Manhattan Institute scholar widely credited with popularizing the 'critical race theory' debate and coining the political use of 'anti-woke' rhetoric, was hired as a key administrator at New College of Florida following the DeSantis-appointed trustee takeover in 2023.

laws.title: Florida Live Local Act
laws.subtitle: Preempting local zoning to mandate affordable housing
laws.fullDescription: Florida's Live Local Act (SB 102, 2023) was a landmark housing law that preempted local zoning ordinances to allow multifamily and mixed-use developments in areas zoned commercial, industrial, or mixed-use if at least 40% of units are affordable (at or below 120% AMI). The law allowed developments to be as tall as the tallest building within a mile, eliminated minimum parking requirements near transit, and streamlined environmental review. It was designed to bypass NIMBY opposition in high-cost coastal cities.
laws.penalty: Local governments that improperly reject applications under the Live Local Act: developer right to sue for mandamus and attorney's fees. Developers who misrepresent affordability compliance: clawback of tax benefits and permit revocation.
exceptions: Properties within 1 mile of a military base subject to height review regardless of adjacent building heights
Projects within established historic districts subject to compatible design review
Environmental overlays (coastal construction zones, wetlands) retain authority over development location

quiz.q: What minimum percentage of units must be affordable for a development to qualify under Florida's Live Local Act?
quiz.explanation: Florida's Live Local Act requires at least 40% of units to be affordable (at or below 120% of Area Median Income) for a development to qualify for the law's zoning preemption benefits — including the ability to build as tall as the tallest nearby building and bypass local zoning restrictions.

laws.title: Stop WOKE Act and Educational Content Restrictions
laws.subtitle: Florida restricts diversity training and classroom instruction
laws.fullDescription: Florida's Individual Freedom Act (Stop WOKE Act) restricted employers and universities from conducting diversity, equity, and inclusion training that could cause individuals to feel guilt or discomfort based on race. Separately, the Parental Rights in Education Act limited classroom instruction on sexual orientation and gender identity. Multiple provisions were challenged in federal court.
laws.penalty: Employers violating Stop WOKE Act: employees can sue for damages; schools violating classroom rules: loss of state funding
exceptions: Factual historical instruction on civil rights permitted
Private sector employers not receiving state funds have different requirements

quiz.q: What common name is Florida's Individual Freedom Act known by?
quiz.explanation: Florida's Individual Freedom Act is commonly known as the 'Stop WOKE Act,' restricting diversity training in workplaces and universities that could make individuals feel discomfort based on their race or sex.

laws.title: Property Insurance Crisis and Citizens Depopulation
laws.subtitle: Florida reforms insurance market after private insurers flee
laws.fullDescription: Florida enacted insurance market reforms after numerous private insurers withdrew from the state or became insolvent due to hurricane losses. Laws limited assignment of benefit claims that had driven up litigation costs, reformed Citizens Property Insurance (state insurer) to push policies to private market, and created a reinsurance fund to stabilise the market. Premiums remained among the highest in the nation.
laws.penalty: Insurance fraud under new anti-assignment rules: criminal prosecution; insurers misrepresenting financial health: regulatory action
exceptions: Low-income homeowners receive subsidised Citizens rates that are not subject to depopulation push
Manufactured homes have separate regulatory treatment

quiz.q: What practice did Florida's insurance reforms restrict to reduce frivolous litigation?
quiz.explanation: Florida's insurance reforms restricted assignment of benefits (AOB) — a practice where homeowners signed over insurance claim rights to contractors, who then filed inflated claims and lawsuits against insurers — which had driven many insurers out of Florida.

laws.title: Florida's Bright Futures Scholarship Restrictions
laws.subtitle: Florida ties college scholarship to workforce shortage majors
laws.fullDescription: Florida enacted reforms to its Bright Futures scholarship programme, which previously provided free tuition to high-achieving students regardless of major. New laws created tiered funding based on whether students chose majors aligned with state workforce needs (STEM, healthcare, trades). Arts, humanities, and social science majors received reduced or no scholarship funding, triggering national debate about education policy.
laws.penalty: No criminal penalties — scholarship reduction is an administrative funding decision
exceptions: Students who subsequently change to approved majors can receive restored funding from their second year
Pre-existing scholarship recipients grandfathered under prior rules

quiz.q: What type of majors does Florida's reformed Bright Futures scholarship prioritise for full funding?
quiz.explanation: Florida's reformed Bright Futures scholarship prioritises STEM (science, technology, engineering, mathematics), healthcare, and trade programmes for full funding, while arts, humanities, and social science majors receive reduced or no scholarship support.

laws.title: Florida Resilience and Hurricane Protection Act
laws.subtitle: Infrastructure hardening and managed coastal retreat
laws.fullDescription: Florida enacted the Climate Resilience and Hurricane Infrastructure Protection Act 2025 following consecutive record hurricane seasons. The law creates a $4 billion Resilient Florida Program for sea wall construction and coastal protection infrastructure, establishes a Voluntary Home Buyout Program for high-risk coastal properties at pre-storm market value using federal and state funds, mandates that new construction within 2,500 feet of mean high-water line use Category 5 hurricane-resistant building standards, requires all coastal municipalities to complete Climate Vulnerability Assessments by 2027, and introduces a Florida Resilience Disclosure requirement for real estate transactions in FEMA Special Flood Hazard Areas.
laws.penalty: Construction without hurricane-resistant certification in coastal zone: stop-work order plus $100,000 per day; false resilience disclosure in property sale: $500,000 civil penalty; failure to complete municipal vulnerability assessment: loss of state infrastructure funding
exceptions: Repairs to existing structures under 50% of assessed value may use previous code standards
Historic structures have modified compliance framework
Agricultural structures exempt from residential coastal building standards

quiz.q: What standard must new construction within 2,500 feet of Florida's coast meet under the Hurricane Protection Act?
quiz.explanation: Florida's Climate Resilience and Hurricane Infrastructure Protection Act requires new construction within 2,500 feet of the coast to meet Category 5 hurricane-resistant building standards — the highest wind resistance designation.

laws.title: Florida Higher Education Autonomy and Accreditation Reform
laws.subtitle: State oversight of universities and accreditation overhaul
laws.fullDescription: Florida enacted the Higher Education Excellence and Accountability Act 2025, extending Governor DeSantis's education reform agenda to university governance and accreditation. The law creates a Florida Accreditation Commission as alternative to national accreditation bodies, requires university faculty senates to include a minimum 30% non-tenure-track membership, mandates that all public universities annually publish 'value rankings' showing graduate employment and earnings outcomes by major, prohibits DEI offices at public institutions from conducting admissions or hiring reviews, establishes a Student Rights Ombudsman with power to investigate perceived viewpoint discrimination, and introduces a 5-year post-tenure review for faculty at public universities.
laws.penalty: University accreditation non-compliance with state commission: loss of state funding; DEI prohibited activity: $500,000 per institution plus removal of responsible administrators; false employment outcome reporting: $2 million fine
exceptions: Private universities retain full accreditation freedom under First Amendment protections
Religious institutions' educational philosophy explicitly exempt from non-discrimination provisions
Medical and law professional schools governed under separate professional accreditation framework

quiz.q: What type of periodic review does Florida's 2025 Higher Education Act require for tenured faculty at public universities?
quiz.explanation: Florida's Higher Education Excellence and Accountability Act introduces a 5-year post-tenure review for faculty at public universities — a mechanism critics argue weakens tenure protections while proponents say increases faculty accountability.

laws.title: Florida Election Law and Voter Roll Maintenance Act
laws.subtitle: Expanding voter verification and third-party registration limits
laws.fullDescription: Florida enacted the Election Integrity Enhancement and Voter Roll Accuracy Act 2025, extending Governor DeSantis's election reform agenda. The law creates the Florida Election Security Unit within the Department of State with criminal investigation powers for voter fraud, mandates annual voter roll cross-checks against Social Security death records, DMV records, and federal databases, restricts third-party voter registration organizations to 14-day submission timelines with $250 penalty per late form (up from $50), creates a proof-of-citizenship requirement for new voter registrations verified through SAVE database, and establishes the Florida Election Code Summary delivered to every registered voter annually.
laws.penalty: Third-party registration submission delay: $250 per form; voter registration fraud: 5 years plus felony disenfranchisement; Election Security Unit obstruction: 10 years imprisonment
exceptions: Motor voter registrations through DMV exempt from citizenship verification (federal law preempts)
Military and overseas voters have simplified re-registration framework
Emergency natural disaster provisions allow registration deadline extensions

quiz.q: What increased fine does Florida's 2025 Election Act impose on third-party voter registration organizations per late-submitted form?
quiz.explanation: Florida's Election Integrity Act increases the fine for third-party voter registration organizations that submit forms late from $50 to $250 per form — a dramatic increase that critics argue burdens voting rights groups while supporters argue it ensures timely submission of registrations.

laws.title: Hurricane Preparedness and Insurance Market Stabilization Act
laws.subtitle: Addressing insurance crisis amid intensifying storms
laws.fullDescription: Florida enacted emergency insurance market legislation after multiple major insurers exited the state due to catastrophic hurricane losses and litigation costs. The law reforms property insurance litigation by limiting attorney fees in insurance disputes, restructures the state-backed Citizens Property Insurance Corporation, mandates hurricane-resistant building codes for new construction in coastal areas, and creates a state reinsurance fund to keep private insurers in the market.
laws.penalty: Insurance fraud in hurricane claims carries up to 15 years imprisonment. Contractors who fraudulently solicit assignment of insurance benefits face professional license revocation and up to five years imprisonment.
exceptions: Mobile homes and manufactured housing have separate compliance timelines for the new building codes
Very low-income homeowners in flood-prone areas receive subsidized Citizens Insurance rates

quiz.q: What problem triggered Florida's Insurance Market Stabilization Act?
options: Multiple major insurers exiting the state due to hurricane losses
A Supreme Court ruling voiding all policies
quiz.explanation: Multiple major property insurers exited the Florida market due to catastrophic hurricane losses and costly litigation, leaving hundreds of thousands of homeowners without coverage or facing massive premium increases.

laws.title: Higher Education Accountability and DEI Restriction Act
laws.subtitle: DeSantis transformation of university governance
laws.fullDescription: Florida enacted sweeping higher education reform legislation restricting diversity, equity and inclusion programs at public universities, eliminating DEI offices, banning certain courses in critical race theory and gender studies from required curricula, and establishing new general education requirements emphasizing Western Civilization. The law also creates post-tenure review for professors and expands political oversight of university hiring.
laws.penalty: State university administrators who maintain prohibited DEI offices face budget cuts and personal disciplinary action. Professors who violate curriculum standards face post-tenure review proceedings that could result in termination.
exceptions: Private universities in Florida are not subject to the DEI restrictions
Elective courses in diverse subjects remain permitted — only required curriculum content is affected

quiz.q: What type of academic programs did Florida's higher education law ban from public universities?
options: Diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) offices and programs
quiz.explanation: Florida's legislation banned DEI offices and programs from public universities, eliminated mandatory DEI training, and restricted certain courses related to race and gender theory — part of a broader conservative effort to reshape higher education.

laws.title: Sea Level Rise Adaptation and Coastal Infrastructure Act
laws.subtitle: Planning for unavoidable coastal flooding
laws.fullDescription: Florida enacted climate adaptation legislation — rare for the state's conservative politics — acknowledging sea level rise projections and mandating action. The law requires sea level rise adaptation plans from all coastal municipalities, creates a state revolving fund for coastal infrastructure upgrades, establishes managed retreat incentives for voluntary relocation from the most vulnerable coastal areas, and updates building codes for new coastal construction.
laws.penalty: Coastal municipalities that fail to submit required adaptation plans lose eligibility for state infrastructure funding. Developers who build below the new elevated coastal standards in high-risk zones face civil liability for flooding damages.
exceptions: Existing legally built structures may remain and be repaired without triggering new coastal adaptation requirements
Agricultural lands in tidal areas retain their current use regardless of sea level rise projections

quiz.q: By how much is sea level projected to rise along Florida's coast by 2060 under moderate scenarios?
quiz.explanation: Moderate sea level rise projections for Florida's coast suggest approximately 6-12 inches of rise by 2060, with higher scenarios possible. Even this modest rise threatens low-lying areas of Miami, Tampa Bay, and the Keys, as storm surges compound the baseline increase.

laws.title: Florida Condo Safety and Surfside Collapse Prevention Act
laws.subtitle: High-Rise Building Inspection Mandatory Law
laws.fullDescription: Mandates structural inspections for all condominium buildings over three stories or 30 years old following the 2021 Champlain Towers South collapse in Surfside that killed 98 people. The law requires milestone inspections, structural integrity reserve studies, and funding of reserves for major repairs. Buildings must complete inspections within specified timelines or face restrictions on habitation.
laws.penalty: Building closure orders for non-compliant condos; fines up to $1,000 per day for associations failing reserve requirements
exceptions: Single-family homes and townhouses exempt
New buildings under 10 years old have extended inspection timeline
laws.sourceLabel: Florida Department of Business and Professional Regulation

quiz.q: What 2021 tragedy drove Florida's Condo Safety Act?
quiz.explanation: The Champlain Towers South collapse in Surfside in 2021, which killed 98 people, drove Florida's mandatory condo inspection law.

laws.title: Florida Live Local Act and Workforce Housing Development Law
laws.subtitle: Affordable Housing and Zoning Override
laws.fullDescription: Creates powerful incentives for workforce housing development by allowing developers to bypass local zoning restrictions for mixed-use projects with affordable units. The law mandates that municipalities approve qualifying projects administratively without public hearings, provides property tax exemptions for affordable units, establishes a state housing fund, and creates expedited permitting for housing in commercial zones.
laws.penalty: Mandamus actions against municipalities blocking qualifying projects; loss of state housing funds for non-compliant cities
exceptions: Coastal high-hazard areas and flood zones excluded
Historic districts retain some local control

quiz.q: What does Florida's Live Local Act allow developers to bypass for housing projects?
quiz.explanation: Florida's Live Local Act allows developers with qualifying affordable housing projects to bypass local zoning restrictions administratively.

laws.title: Florida Digital Bill of Rights and Consumer Data Privacy Act
laws.subtitle: Personal Data Protection and Tech Company Regulation Law
laws.fullDescription: Establishes comprehensive consumer data privacy rights for Florida residents with specific provisions for large technology companies. The law creates rights to access, delete, and correct personal data, mandates opt-out rights for data sales, establishes special protections for children under 18, creates the right to opt out of profiling and targeted advertising, and establishes an enforcement mechanism through the Florida Department of Legal Affairs.
laws.penalty: Civil penalties up to $50,000 per violation; up to $100,000 per intentional violation; class action rights
exceptions: Small businesses with less than $1 billion global revenue have simplified compliance
B2B data without consumer information not covered

quiz.q: What age threshold does Florida's Digital Bill of Rights establish for special data protections for minors?
quiz.explanation: Florida's Digital Bill of Rights establishes special data privacy protections for children under 18, stronger than federal COPPA protections.

laws.title: Florida Social Media Parental Consent and Child Protection Act
laws.subtitle: Under-16 Social Media Age Restriction Law
laws.fullDescription: Requires parental consent for children under 16 to create social media accounts and mandates age verification. The law requires social media companies to verify users' ages using technical methods, mandates deletion of accounts of users found to be underage without consent, creates parental controls dashboard requirements, and establishes the Florida Department of Legal Affairs' enforcement authority.
laws.penalty: Civil penalties up to $50,000 per knowing violation against minors; class actions for pattern violations
exceptions: Educational platforms with parental notification
Communications services not primarily social media

quiz.q: What age threshold requires parental consent for social media under Florida's act?
quiz.explanation: Florida's Social Media Parental Consent Act requires parental consent for children under 16 to create social media accounts.

laws.title: Higher Education Restrictions on DEI Programs
laws.subtitle: Florida Eliminates DEI Offices at Public Universities
laws.fullDescription: Florida eliminated diversity, equity, and inclusion programs at public universities, banning DEI offices, mandatory DEI training, and funding for DEI-related activities. The law was part of Governor DeSantis's broader education culture war agenda.
laws.penalty: State funding reductions for non-compliant universities
exceptions: Federal compliance requirements still apply
Student organizations may voluntarily maintain DEI activities

quiz.q: What did Florida's law ban at public universities?
quiz.explanation: Florida banned DEI programs at public universities including offices, mandatory training, and funding for DEI activities.

laws.title: Condo Safety Law Post-Surfside Collapse
laws.subtitle: Florida Requires Structural Inspections for Aging Buildings
laws.fullDescription: Following the 2021 Champlain Towers South collapse in Surfside that killed 98 people, Florida enacted comprehensive condominium safety legislation requiring milestone inspections for buildings over 3 stories and 30 years old, structural integrity reserve studies, and mandatory reserve funding. The law imposed significant costs on condo owners.
laws.penalty: Fines for associations not complying; county enforcement authority
exceptions: Newer buildings on different schedule
